picks.style: roman comic canticum, tibia and plucked lyre, sardonic female voice, brisk, worldly
picks.why: Syra's advice to plunder, fleece and rend every man you lay hold of — a complete comic argument in two voices.

picks.style: roman monody, soft double pipe and lyre, warm low female voice, reflective, unhurried
picks.why: The courtesan's soliloquy: the ring recognised, the truth out, and "I never, for the sake of gain, will give my mind to base actions".

picks.style: rustic satyr chorus, panpipes and goatskin drum, rough male voices with calls and whistles, lively, pastoral
picks.why: The goat-herding chorus — dewy slope, bursting udder, bleating kids — a genuine work-song with shouts built into it.

picks.style: greek drinking song, aulos and clapping hands, slurred lusty male voice, rollicking, accelerating
picks.why: Silenus on wine: love with all its frolic, dancing, and oblivion of woe — "if a man rejoice not in his drinking, he is mad".

picks.style: grotesque satyr chorus, braying pipes and heavy drums, leering voices in unison, gleeful, macabre
picks.why: "Ope wide the portal of thy gaping throat, Cyclops" — a cannibal serenade, self-contained and horribly catchy.

picks.style: underworld invocation, low drones and struck metal, bass male voice, sepulchral, slow, spoken-sung
picks.why: Thyestes' ghost arriving: "I flee the underworld; I put the upper world to flight" — an opening that explains itself entirely.

picks.style: roman chorus, lyre and low strings, unison voices, grave, measured, resigned
picks.why: "Whatever Fortune has raised on high, she lifts to dash it down" — and the safer joy of rowing close to shore.

picks.style: lament with responding chorus, harp and viol over a drone, solo female voice, slow, aching
picks.why: Cassandra refusing company in her grief against the chorus's "it is sweet to mingle tears with tears" — call and answer already written in.

picks.style: 18th century ode for music, baroque strings and trumpet, tenor with small chorus, alternating grand and tender
picks.why: The Power of Poetry — Orpheus stilling the swains, Rapine dropping her prey. Written in ode stanzas that already ask for setting.

picks.style: georgian moral air, harpsichord and violin, wry baritone, brisk, epigrammatic
picks.why: The fool with the fiddle — "There's musick in it, could I fetch it out" — and the moral that we lack not instruments but art.

picks.style: english drinking-and-repenting song, fortepiano and cello, rueful tenor, easy, self-mocking
picks.why: "To-day be happy, and to-morrow wise!" and the confession that to fail, the first step is to vow.

picks.style: georgian song in tetrameter couplets, harpsichord and flute, arch light soprano, playful, trotting
picks.why: Cupid complaining of his own portraits: the patriot enslaved to a jilt, the sage wedded to a shrew, vestals languishing for a beau.

picks.style: 18th century ode, strings and oboe, declamatory soprano, stately, indignant
picks.why: Phoebus growing jealous as the Muses build a woman's mind and denying her the universal tongue — the grievance is fully legible.

picks.style: sea epic recitation, bowed drone and deep frame drum, resonant male voice, vast, foreboding, slow swell
picks.why: Pedo's Ocean: "Whither are we borne?" — mortals forbidden to know the end of things, troubling the gods' quiet waters with oars.

picks.style: roman funeral declamation, low strings and muffled drum, grave male voice, heavy, mournful
picks.why: Cicero's head on the Rostra — "one day took away the glory of a lifetime" and the Latin tongue fell silent.

picks.style: oracular chant, drone and struck bowl, high wavering female voice, hypnotic, portentous
picks.why: Only candidate, but it carries a whole oracle in verse — flames from burning seas, an island reared up dreadful to hear — plus the Castalian springs.

picks.style: aeolic lyric, solo lyre, clear unadorned female voice, intimate, spare
picks.why: Only candidate, and it is Sappho answering: if your wish were good, shame would not have filled your eyes. One closed thought.
